paragraphs.heading: Ice that stays put
paragraphs.text: Fast ice is frozen sea or lake water that is held in one place. It may be anchored to the coast, to shoals on the sea floor, or to icebergs that have run aground. People also call it land-fast, landfast or shore-fast ice. It can grow where it sits as the water freezes, or it can build up when drifting pieces of ice freeze onto the shore or some other anchor. Unlike drift ice, also called pack ice, it does not travel with the winds and currents.

paragraphs.heading: How wide and how deep
paragraphs.text: The band of fast ice along a coast usually comes and goes with the seasons, and its width changes with it. That width depends on how thick the ice is and on the shape of the sea floor and the nearby islands. It can be only a few meters across or reach several hundred kilometers. How far it spreads out to sea depends mainly on the water depth, how sheltered the shore is, the time of year, and how hard the pack ice presses against it. In Arctic seas it reaches out to water 20 m deep, while in Subarctic seas it stops at about 10 m.

paragraphs.heading: Where it cannot form
paragraphs.text: Some coasts get no fast ice at all. Where the shelf drops away steeply and there are no islands, as in the Sea of Okhotsk off Hokkaidō, the tides keep it from forming. The reverse also happens. A smaller ocean basin may hold only a fast ice zone, with no pack ice in it.

paragraphs.heading: Its surface and its parts
paragraphs.text: The surface of fast ice can be smooth and level, or rugged where it has been put under great pressure. Right at the shore lies the ice foot, made by water freezing again and again between ebb tides. Tidal cracks split the ice foot off from the rest of the fast ice. Farther from the coast, the ice can become anchored to the sea bottom itself, and then it is called bottomfast ice.

paragraphs.heading: Age and edges
paragraphs.text: Fast ice does not always vanish in summer. When it lasts through one or more melting seasons, it is sorted by age in the usual way, as first-year, second-year or multiyear ice. Its outer limit, where it meets the drifting pack ice, is called the fast ice boundary, and in places a shear ridge runs along it. Fast ice can also border or enclose pressure ridges that reach down far enough to sit on the bottom, and these grounded ridges are known as stamukhi.
